_readme: Client requests for information (RFIs). Each daily run re-checks CISA KEV and the day's stories against `keywords` and shows what is new. This file is published on a public site: use client codenames, never real names.

rfis.bluf: Two critical PHP bugs let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a web server. Fixes shipped on 21 October, details leaked a day earlier, and vendors report attacks already under way. Patch every internet-facing PHP system now, then check it was not compromised before the patch.
rfis.confidence: High confidence on the facts: the CVE records and CISA KEV (catalogue 2026.10.21) were checked directly on 22 October. Exploitation reports come from vendors (Cloudflare, Patchstack) and are not yet confirmed by CISA.

findings.title: What is affected
findings.text: Any PHP that serves web requests: PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php (highest risk), php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. Fixed in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and older are end of life, so only a vendor backport (for example a Linux distribution or Plesk build dated 21 October) protects them. PHP is also bundled inside hosting panels, appliances and products like WordPress hosting, so suppliers must be asked.

findings.title: Exploitation
findings.text: Amazon's honeypots recorded an exploitation attempt on 17 October, four days before disclosure, and Amazon cannot explain how the attacker had the details. Details then leaked publicly on 20 October and proof-of-concept code appeared on 21 October. Cloudflare saw early attack attempts and deployed emergency WAF rules, and Patchstack reports attacks are ongoing. Not yet on CISA KEV (catalogue 2026.10.21). Some public exploit code is unverified and may itself contain malware.

findings.title: What an attack looks like
findings.text: Very large form POSTs (about 3.5 MB field names, null bytes). PHP error log: 'Allowed memory size of ... bytes exhausted (tried to allocate ...) in Unknown on line 0'. Apache: 'AH00052: child pid ... exit signal Segmentation fault (11)'. The clearest sign of success is a web worker (php-fpm, apache2, httpd) starting a shell or connecting out. A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 with no crash, so absence of errors proves nothing.

findings.title: Network detection
findings.text: Network detection: Cisco Talos Snort rules 67359 and 67360 cover both CVEs (also in the free Community Ruleset). They can only inspect traffic they can read, so HTTPS between a CDN or WAF and the web server hides attacks from a network IDS in front of that server.

rfis.assessment: It is almost certain (95% and above) that internet-facing unpatched PHP sites will be attacked in the coming days. It is likely (55-75%) that CISA adds these CVEs to KEV soon. A site patched after 17 October could already have been compromised, so patching alone is not enough.

cves.issue: Remote code execution via out-of-memory handling corruption
Remote code execution via stale global state (use after free); memory disclosure

actions: Find every PHP system, internet-facing first, including PHP bundled in third-party products and hosting.
Upgrade to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 (or later) and restart all PHP workers. For 8.1 and older, get written confirmation of a vendor backport or migrate.
If an internet-facing system cannot be patched quickly, put a WAF block on oversized POST bodies or take it offline (NCSC advice).
Hunt for compromise since 17 October: web workers spawning shells, new PHP files in web roots, outbound connections from web servers, and the memory and crash errors above.
Google SecOps: confirm the Mandiant Frontline Threats curated rule pack is enabled (23 new detections), and check Emerging Threat Center entry GLOBAL.26.015 where licensed.

Where the website is run by a supplier, ask them to confirm the patched version, the restart, and the result of their own log review, and to share Cloudflare security events if you want them reviewed.

hunts.name: 1. Web worker starts a shell or download tool (UDM search)
hunts.why: Strongest sign of successful exploitation. Needs Linux endpoint telemetry (EDR or auditd) from the web servers.
hunts.query:
metadata.event_type = "PROCESS_LAUNCH"
AND principal.process.file.full_path = /(php-fpm|php-cgi|lsphp|frankenphp|httpd|apache2)/ nocase
AND target.process.file.full_path = /\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|perl|nc|ncat|socat|busybox)$/ nocase

hunts.name: 2. Same, as a YARA-L detection rule
hunts.why: Save as a rule so it alerts from now on.
hunts.query:
rule php2shell_worker_spawns_shell {
  meta:
    description = "PHP or web worker launching a shell or download tool (PHP2Shell post-exploitation)"
    severity = "HIGH"
  events:
    $e.metadata.event_type = "PROCESS_LAUNCH"
    $e.principal.process.file.full_path = /(php-fpm|php-cgi|lsphp|frankenphp|httpd|apache2)/ nocase
    $e.target.process.file.full_path = /\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|perl|nc|ncat|socat|busybox)$/ nocase
  condition:
    $e
}

hunts.name: 3. New PHP files written by the web server (UDM search)
hunts.query:
metadata.event_type = "FILE_CREATION"
AND target.file.full_path = /\/(var\/www|srv\/www|public_html|htdocs|wp-content)\/.*\.(php|phtml|phar)$/ nocase
AND principal.process.file.full_path = /(php-fpm|php-cgi|lsphp|httpd|apache2|nginx)/ nocase

hunts.name: 4. Exploit attempts in PHP and Apache error logs (raw log search, regex)
hunts.why: Needs PHP or Apache error logs ingested. Errors alone are not proof; correlate with oversized POSTs.
hunts.query:
Allowed memory size of \d+ bytes exhausted.*in Unknown on line 0
AH00052: child pid \d+ exit signal Segmentation fault \(11\)
child \d+ exited on signal 11 \(SIGSEGV

hunts.name: 5. Oversized POST requests (UDM search, web proxy, WAF or load balancer logs)
hunts.why: The out-of-memory exploit uses multi-megabyte form posts. Which byte field holds the request size depends on the log source.

hunts.name: 6. Outbound connections from web workers (UDM search)
hunts.why: Reverse shells and downloads. Exclude your own ranges and known update servers.

hunts.name: 7. IDS alerts for the Talos PHP2Shell rules (UDM search)
hunts.why: Works for any Snort-based IDS feeding the SIEM, including Cisco and Meraki, where signature IDs look like 1:67359:1. Only sees unencrypted traffic.

updates.note: Opened after the NCSC alert. CVE records and CISA KEV checked directly (not on KEV yet). Detection guidance from Google Cloud, Datadog and Cisco Talos added as hunt queries. Client B response coordinated with the SOC partner.
Compromise-check window moved back to 17 October after Amazon Threat Intelligence reported an exploitation attempt four days before disclosure. Still not on CISA KEV.

rfis.bluf: No Okta or Auth0 vulnerability is known to be exploited. The real risk to Okta customers is social engineering: phone-call phishing (vishing) that tricks staff or the help desk into handing over sign-ins and MFA.
rfis.confidence: Moderate confidence. CISA KEV (catalogue 2026.10.08) and the CVE records were checked directly on 12 October; Okta's own advisory pages could not be reached and are cited from search results.

findings.title: Patch batch: September 2026 advisories
findings.text: On 8 September 2026 Okta published fixes for nine bugs in its self-hosted components, found by scanning its own code with AI. Okta reports no evidence of exploitation, and none are on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list (re-checked 12 October, catalogue 2026.10.08). Okta's cloud service is patched by Okta; customers only need to act if they run the components below.

findings.title: Active threat: vishing against Okta SSO
findings.text: Since January 2026, groups linked to ShinyHunters, Scattered Spider and Lapsus$ ('Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters') have called staff and IT help desks, steering victims through fake Okta login pages in real time to capture passwords and MFA approvals. Push MFA with number matching does not stop it. Once inside Okta, they move into connected SaaS apps (Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) and steal data for extortion. Reported targets include financial services. Latest tradecraft (September): attackers keep access by enrolling their own Okta FastPass device, often an emulated Android phone, so a password reset alone does not remove them.

rfis.assessment: It is unlikely (25-35%) that the September Okta bugs are being exploited at scale today, but a realistic possibility (40-50%) that exploitation follows now that details are public. It is highly likely (80-90%) that vishing against Okta-using organisations continues through the rest of 2026.

cves.issue: Stored cross-site scripting in the admin panel
Local privilege escalation to code execution
OAuth client secret written to logs in plain text
SAML assertion written to logs after MFA
SSH target treated as a command-line option
Pass-through auth trusts a client-supplied header (only if that optional source is enabled)

actions: Check whether you run any of the listed self-hosted components and upgrade them to the fixed versions.
If you used the Hyperdrive installer, rotate the OAuth client secret and clear old installer and agent logs, since they may hold secrets or SAML assertions.
Move admins and help desk staff to phishing-resistant MFA (Okta FastPass, FIDO2 security keys or passkeys), then everyone else.
Use Okta network zones to allow sign-ins only from expected networks and block anonymisers (VPNs, Tor, proxies).
Tighten help desk checks before any password or MFA reset, for example a call back to a known number or manager approval.
Alert on new Okta FastPass or authenticator enrolments, especially from emulated or unrecognised Android devices, and review existing enrolments after any suspected compromise.
Watch the Okta System Log for new MFA enrolments or resets, sign-ins from new devices or locations, and new admin role grants, and alert on them.
Block the Okta-themed malware URLs listed above (defanged) and warn Okta admins and developers not to download Okta tooling from unofficial GitHub repositories.

sources.name: Help Net Security: Okta warns of real-time vishing kits (Jan 2026)
The Register: ShinyHunters claims Okta customer breaches (Jan 2026)

updates.note: Request received and researched. No Okta or Auth0 CVE on CISA KEV; eight September CVEs documented; vishing campaign assessed as the main risk.

Re-checked: still nothing on CISA KEV and no Okta stories in the daily feeds (5 to 11 October). Added CVE-2026-78560 from the same September batch and the FastPass persistence tradecraft. Okta-themed indicators (for example fake Okta login domains) are now scanned for every morning in URLhaus and ThreatFox. First result: URLhaus lists a malware download disguised as an 'okta-terraform-demo-template' on GitHub (hxxps://raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/fdaloiapp/okta-terraform-demo-template/...), a lure aimed at Okta admins and developers. Added to the blocklist recommendation.
